title: Authorization policy lives in the document's own auth scope as replicated grants, so reducers carry no access-control code
content:
Since v6.2.2-dev.74 the reactor can decide who may do what from a policy stored **on the document itself**, in its `auth` scope. The policy is a list of **grants** folded by a platform reducer exactly like any other state, so it syncs, replays and converges the way document content does.

The consequence for model authors is the headline: **reducers contain no authorization code**. The Cookbook's `document-acl` recipe is built as the deliberate counterpart to `role-based-auth` — same outcome (callers gated per operation), opposite mechanism. In `role-based-auth` every reducer starts with signer checks and the rules are baked into the model; in `document-acl` the reducers throw only domain errors (`DuplicateEntry`, `EntryNotFound`), read the signer solely to record an entry's `author`, and the rules are **data** — inspectable, replicated, and changeable at runtime without touching the model.

The spec's motivation names the problem this solves: authorization used to live either outside the reactor (middleware, the GraphQL layer) or inside reducers, so the same logic was written in several places and whole classes of policy were impossible. Pulling it into the core lets it ride on the guarantees the reactor already provides — the event log, synchronization, signatures — and gives consistency guarantees an external gate cannot: a refused write is refused **at admission**, fails the job with `AuthorizationDeniedError`, and stores nothing; the reducer never runs.

Two boundaries to keep straight. Enforcement is staged behind feature flags and bites only on documents whose policy was initialized (an uninitialized policy allows everything). And this is a *second* authorization system next to the host's permission tables, answering a different question — see the note on the two systems.
